name: The Red-Black Tree
statement: Keep a search tree balanced by coloring nodes red or black under rules that bound its height.
statementAccent: coloring nodes red or black under rules that bound its height
meaning: A red-black tree is a kind of self-balancing binary search tree. Each node stores one extra bit representing its colour, either red or black, and the tree uses these colours, maintained through a set of properties, to keep itself approximately balanced during insertions and deletions, guaranteeing order log n time for search, insertion, and deletion. The colouring is governed by a few invariants: every node is either red or black; by common convention the root is black; the null leaf nodes are treated as black; a red node's children must both be black, so no two red nodes appear consecutively on a path; and every path from a given node down to any of its descendant null leaves passes through the same number of black nodes, a quantity called the black height. Together these constraints ensure that the longest root-to-leaf path is no more than twice the length of the shortest, so the tree stays approximately balanced and its height is order log n. When an insertion or deletion violates the properties, they are restored by recolouring nodes and by rotations, local restructurings that pivot a node with its child while preserving the search order. The structure originated with Rudolf Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-trees, and the red-black colour convention and name were introduced by Leonidas Guibas and Robert Sedgewick in 1978. Red-black trees are very widely used to implement ordered maps and sets, including the C++ standard library's map and set, Java's TreeMap and TreeSet, and structures in the Linux kernel.
mechanism: A red-black tree guarantees balance not by measuring subtree heights directly, as an AVL tree does, but by colouring nodes and enforcing rules that indirectly cap how unbalanced the tree can get. The invariants are the heart of it. Every node is coloured red or black; the null leaves are black; a red node may not have a red child, so reds never appear two in a row along a path; and, crucially, every path from any node to the null leaves below it contains the same number of black nodes, its black height. From these it follows that no root-to-leaf path can be more than twice as long as any other: the shortest possible path is all black, and the longest alternates black and red, so with equal black counts the longest is at most double the shortest. That bound forces the tree's height to be logarithmic in the number of nodes, which is what makes search, insertion, and deletion run in order log n time. Insertion and deletion proceed as in an ordinary binary search tree but can violate the colour rules, for instance by creating two adjacent red nodes or unbalancing the black heights; the tree repairs itself through two operations. Recolouring flips node colours to fix local violations, and rotations, left or right, pivot a parent and child to restructure the tree while preserving the binary search order of the keys. A bounded number of rotations, at most a couple for insertion and a few for deletion, plus recolouring along the path to the root, suffice to restore all invariants after any single update, so modifications stay order log n. Because red-black trees permit somewhat looser balance than AVL trees, they perform fewer rotations on updates, which favours insertion- and deletion-heavy workloads, at the cost of slightly deeper trees and marginally slower lookups.

whyItMatters: The red-black tree is one of the most widely deployed data structures in practical software, the default implementation of ordered maps and sets in major standard libraries, and it does essential, invisible work in countless programs. Its value is a guarantee: by colouring nodes and enforcing a handful of invariants, it ensures that a dynamic collection of keys stays balanced no matter what order elements are inserted or deleted, so search, insertion, and deletion always run in order log n time, never degrading into the linear-time behaviour that an unbalanced binary search tree can suffer. This reliability, combined with efficient updates, is why red-black trees underlie the C++ standard library's std::map and std::set, Java's TreeMap and TreeSet, and important structures in the Linux kernel, such as its process scheduler. Compared with the stricter AVL tree, the red-black tree balances a little more loosely and performs fewer rotations when the tree changes, making it especially well suited to workloads with many insertions and deletions, which is common in systems code. It is also a landmark in the theory of data structures, an elegant demonstration that a few local colour rules can enforce global balance, with a lineage from Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-trees to the red-black formulation of Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978. As the search tree kept balanced by red and black colouring rules, the red-black tree is a cornerstone of ordered-container implementations.

working.text: assign each node red or black, with null leaves black and, by convention, the root black.
forbid two reds in a row and require equal black counts on every root-to-leaf path.
after inserting or deleting, restore the invariants by recolouring and rotations, keeping height order log n.

limits: The red-black tree is robust but several points reward care. It guarantees only approximate balance, not the tightest possible: the longest path may be nearly twice the shortest, so red-black trees are somewhat taller than AVL trees and their lookups slightly slower; the trade is that they rotate less on updates, favouring modification-heavy workloads, so red-black and AVL trees suit different profiles and neither is universally best. The invariants themselves carry nuance: the property that the root is black is a common convention rather than a defining structural requirement in every formulation, and different textbooks list the properties slightly differently, so counting or stating them loosely can mislead. Red-black trees are more complex to implement correctly than plain binary search trees, and deletion in particular is intricate. Like any comparison-based ordered structure, they are generally slower than a hash table for pure key lookup and are valuable for the ordering they preserve. Some historical details reward care: the structure descends from Rudolf Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-trees, and the red-black colouring and name are due to Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978. So the red-black tree robustly guarantees order log n ordered operations, understood as an approximately balanced, update-friendly structure whose exact invariants and conventions should be stated with care.
misreadings: The red-black tree is not perfectly balanced; its longest path can be nearly twice its shortest, and it is looser than an AVL tree. The root-is-black rule is a convention, not a universal structural law. And it is not faster than a hash table for pure lookup, being valuable for order, so treating it as optimally balanced, as fixed in its exact properties across all texts, or as a lookup-speed champion, misreads it.
origin: The self-balancing binary search tree using red and black node colours, derived from Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-trees and given its red-black formulation by Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978, guaranteeing order log n operations.
